What does one event actually tell you about the scene?
One way to say it
A pixel reports that its log brightness has changed by a threshold since its last reset. The event gives the location, time, and sign of that change. It measures a relative change; both motion and changing illumination can produce it.
Keep these ideas
threshold crossing · local reference · motion or illumination
If pressed

The ideal rule uses fixed contrast thresholds. Threshold variation and other sensor errors enter the observation-model discussion.

Why do events leave a brightness baseline undetermined?
One way to say it
Adding a constant to a pixel's entire log-brightness history preserves all its changes, provided its reset reference shifts with it. The temporal difference model therefore determines the history only up to an additive level. The regularizer chooses that level; a measured reference could supply physical information about it.
Keep these ideas

If pressed

Independent per-pixel offsets in log intensity correspond to independent multiplicative brightness factors after exponentiation.

Why is representing the event stream part of the mathematical model?
One way to say it
Raw events are a signed point measure. Binning, smoothing, interpolation, or timestamp fitting turns them into the quantities used in our residuals. Those choices determine which information survives and how errors enter the estimator, so they are part of the model we analyze.
Keep these ideas

If pressed

The flow theorem begins with fixed represented coefficients. It needs a separate preprocessing bound to become a raw-event stability theorem.

What does well-posedness buy you when the estimate might still be inaccurate?
One way to say it
It gives an estimate that exists, is unique, and changes continuously with the specified inputs. That makes the model's answer determinate and controlled. Accuracy also depends on whether the observations identify the physical quantity and whether the model's assumptions and regularization describe the scene well.

What do the temporal kernels change, and what do they preserve?
One way to say it
A kernel distributes an event's signed contribution across time bins. Unit mass preserves its total contribution when the full support is included, while the width controls how far the influence spreads. The difference operator stays fixed; the observations and any weights derived from them can change.
Keep these ideas
signed unit contribution · temporal spread · same difference operator
If pressed

A kernel crossing the observation-window boundary needs boundary treatment to preserve the full mass identity.

Why is the cumulative event signal naturally BV rather than H-one?
One way to say it
Accumulating finitely many signed events gives a staircase with finite total variation. A nonzero jump contributes an atom to its distributional derivative. H-one would require a square-integrable derivative, so a genuine jump belongs naturally in bounded variation instead.
Keep these ideas
staircase · atomic derivative · finite variation
If pressed

At positive smoothing width, the kernels used here give a square-integrable driver and an H-one primitive.

column2:
Temporal reconstruction · Core rehearsal · T24
When does an accumulated event count approximate a change in brightness?
One way to say it
Under the ideal threshold rule each event marks a log-brightness change of one threshold. So the signed count between two times approximates the change in log brightness divided by the threshold. The exact Chapter 2 identity names three discrepancies: kernel mass crossing a bin boundary, overshoot at each event, and sub-threshold change since the pixel's last event. When those are small, A f approximately y models brightness changes; the absolute level still comes from the model.
Keep these ideas
one threshold per event · three error terms · changes, not levels
If pressed

A missed or spurious event makes one overshoot term as large as the threshold. The regularized solution adds its data residual as a fourth discrepancy, and larger weights enlarge it.

One way to say it

One way to say it
The penalty deliberately pulls the estimate toward smaller profiles. Even with exact increments, that changes the recovered nonconstant modes and fixes the invisible baseline. Reconstruction error therefore contains both this shrinkage bias and propagated observation error; increasing regularization trades more shrinkage for stronger noise control.

What is actually computed after you write down the temporal objective?
One way to say it
Differentiating gives one positive-definite linear system per pixel. We solve those independent systems in parallel to obtain temporal histories. At any reconstruction time, taking that time sample from each history assembles an image. The optimization variable is the whole history, even though the output is displayed as frames.
Keep these ideas
normal equations · independent pixel solves · assemble time slices
If pressed

I developed and used a native C++/CUDA DV version for live windowed reconstruction. Workload, temporal samples, observation window, and output cadence govern responsiveness; fine event timestamps and camera-to-display latency are different quantities.

One way to say it
Instead of fitting each pixel history independently, we ask one static scene to explain observations along a known camera trajectory. We project that scene at each time and then difference the projections. A positive ridge makes the fixed-motion scene solve unique and stable, while the projection sequence determines its invisible scene directions.
Keep these ideas
one scene · known projections then differences · ridge controls invisible directions
If pressed

SAR means synthetic aperture radar. Here the transferred idea is combining moving-sensor observations into one scene estimate; camera motion is supplied to the model.

How does your temporal method relate to the Antil–Sayre bilevel approach?
Answer aloud in your own words, then reveal.
column2:
Temporal reconstruction · Core rehearsal · T23
How does your temporal method relate to the Antil–Sayre bilevel approach?
One way to say it
Our method uses events to set activity-based magnitude penalties and then solves a fixed convex temporal problem. Antil and Sayre use events with intensity frames and an outer optimization of a blur-kernel parameter z for each pixel and frame. The comparison therefore concerns complete approaches with different information and optimization variables, as well as different guarantees.
Keep these ideas
event-only weights · frame-assisted threshold optimization · different guarantees
If pressed

Our fixed positive diagonal gives a unique global quadratic minimizer. The cited bilevel analysis gives existence and conditional local uniqueness under its assumptions. Reported averages, bilevel versus event-only: indoors PSNR 15.37 versus 10.85 with condition numbers 39755 versus 25.51; outdoors PSNR 8.41 versus 8.71 with 39755 versus 27.10.

Your weights are computed from the data. Is the estimator you actually run stable?
Answer aloud in your own words, then reveal.
column2:
Temporal reconstruction · Core rehearsal · T25
Your weights are computed from the data. Is the estimator you actually run stable?
One way to say it
Yes, it is locally Lipschitz. Each Chapter 2 rule maps activity to a weight between a positive floor and a ceiling, and is Lipschitz in the activity. Subtracting the two normal equations gives the fixed-weight data term plus the change in squared weights acting on the second solution. Bounding both inverses by the floor gives a bound that is Lipschitz on bounded sets of data.
Keep these ideas
floor, ceiling, Lipschitz rule · two terms after subtraction · Lipschitz on bounded data
If pressed

The constants are pessimistic because the floor enters cubed. Chapter 4's weights depend on the current profile, so that estimator is a fixed point and uses the contraction condition instead.

column2:
Optical flow · Core rehearsal · V01
Explain the aperture problem to a mathematician outside vision.
One way to say it
A straight edge reveals only its speed perpendicular to itself. Sliding it along itself produces the same local brightness history, so the tangential component stays free. In velocity space, a separate plot from the image, that edge becomes a constraint line: every velocity with the observed normal component. A second edge orientation gives a second line, and if both edges share the motion, the two lines cross at one velocity.
Keep these ideas
normal measured · tangent free · constraint lines in velocity space cross
If pressed

The ideal example assumes steady illumination, matching sensor references, and no visible endpoints or other distinguishing features in the local window.

Optical flow · Core rehearsal · V02
Derive the time-surface motion constraint in a few sentences.
One way to say it
The crossing-time map tells us when the edge reaches each location. Along a point translating with that edge, its crossing time equals the current time. Differentiating along the trajectory says that crossing-time gradient dotted with velocity equals one. The gradient measures slowness in the measured direction.

follow crossing trajectory · chain rule · gradient is slowness
If pressed

This gives one scalar constraint on a two-component velocity. A large crossing-time gradient corresponds to slow normal motion. Scale example: an edge that takes 10 ms to cross one pixel moves at 100 px/s normal to itself.

What directional information does the structure tensor add?
One way to say it
It pools outer products of nearby space-time gradients with nonnegative weights. Each contribution is a squared directional constraint, so the tensor is positive semidefinite. Nonparallel spatial gradients can constrain both velocity components locally; the unified theorem only requires enough information across the connected domain.

Its spatial block supplies data curvature, the space-time cross terms supply forcing, and the final temporal term is constant in velocity.

column2:
Optical flow · Core rehearsal · V18
How do you prove stability of the flow estimate to its coefficients?

Holding the left data and parameters fixed, each candidate cost is quadratic in its right observation, with gradient 2P times the displacement from c and Hessian 2P, and the norm of P is at most one half. So a perturbation xi changes a cost by at most the distance to c times the size of xi, plus half its square. If the largest such change is below half the margin, the winner is preserved.
Keep these ideas
quadratic cost in the right observation · norm of P at most one half · eta below half the margin
If pressed

The bound must include the original winner, whose ideal profile may also be perturbed. Changes to the left data or adaptive parameters add further terms to eta.

Where does the IRLS contraction constant come from?
One way to say it
Subtract two frozen-weight solves: the difference is an inverse-system operator applied to a weight change times a residual. Three estimates bound it: the penalty bounds the operator by one over the square root of ell, the smallest eigenvalue of Lambda transpose Lambda; comparing with the zero profile bounds the weighted residual by the weighted data; reciprocal weights change by at most the prediction change times the two weights, each at most one over epsilon. Together q equals norm A times norm y over root ell times epsilon to the three halves.

If pressed

Pairing the weight change with the weighted residual is what produces the three-halves power. With norm A equal to root g max, q falls below one when the data norm is below lambda min times epsilon to the three halves over root g max; at q of one or more this bound is inconclusive.

Why not train a neural network?
One way to say it
A trained network is also a regularized estimator: where the events leave the answer free, it fills the gap from training images, and these methods fill it with an analyzed penalty. The dissertation identifies those free directions: the per-pixel offset, the flow component along an edge, and disparities with coincident profiles. The two combine: learning the weights in a bilevel problem has a well-defined, smooth lower level, because each fixed-weight solve is unique and smooth in the weights.

On public flow and stereo benchmarks learned methods report the lowest errors; the dissertation asks what the data determine and when each estimator is stable. Event reconstruction has no agreed standard, because frame-image scores assume a brightness level the events leave open.

Your contrast-maximization ridge is 2 epsilon over M, which vanishes as the knots are refined. Does coercivity degrade?
One way to say it
Only in coefficient space. The cubic B-splines are nonnegative and sum to one, so the squared spline is at most a basis-weighted average of squared coefficients; integrating gives the L2 norm at most h squared times the coefficient norm. So the ridge controls 2 epsilon over M h squared times the L2 norm, and M h squared tends to the domain area. With the eigenvalue floor on the gradient, the regularizer controls the H1 norm uniformly in h.
Keep these ideas

If pressed

The coefficient condition number still grows like h to the minus two, standard for an H1 Galerkin matrix with a mass term. With nonuniform knots, weight the ridge by basis integrals to keep it a lumped mass term.

Is there one mechanism behind your temporal, flow, and stereo uniqueness results?
One way to say it
Yes, a complementarity lemma. One quadratic term controls every direction except a finite-dimensional set of modes; the other term must see those modes. Then the sum is coercive, with a constant that falls linearly in how well the second term sees them. In time the data miss the baseline and the penalty fixes it; in flow smoothness misses a uniform pan and the edges fix it; in stereo the data and coupling leave a common constant and the penalty fixes it.
Keep these ideas

If pressed

The condition is also necessary when the missed modes are exactly the kernel. Correspondence selection and contrast maximization sit outside the lemma: one compares finitely many costs, the other is nonconvex.
